newsitem.title: GERMANY: Change afoot in Bundesbank policy, but not this week.
newsitem.headline: Change afoot in Bundesbank policy, but not this week.

text.p: The tide is turning for Bundesbank monetary policy, yet economists are increasingly sceptical that the powerful central bank will allow itself to be scared into raising rates in the middle of its summer break.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing has made clear in recent interviews that the central bank is starting to 'think tight' on policy, referring to growing price pressures, high capacity utilisation and the prolonged weakness of the mark.
Such talk has heightened the view that a rate rise is looming on the horizon after five years of easier policy.
But with the ebullient dollar currently on a receding path, scepticism is rife that the best time for a move is this week.

"The Bundesbank is stocking up on munitions but is keeping its powder dry," analysts at Societe Generale said in a commentary. "It prefers to keep a psychological stranglehold on the market... We see no change in policy over the summer."

The Bundesbank itself triggered an intense period of speculation about the course of its future policy on July 24, when its policy-making council departed for its summer holidays deliberately leaving its policy options open.

Marking a change from the recent established pattern, the central bank did not announce the level for its main money market rate, the repo, throughout the summer holiday, setting it instead only for the first two weeks of the four-week break.
Now, almost two weeks later, the first repo at as yet unannounced conditions is due to be set, with the announcement expected to come on Tuesday morning at about 0700 GMT.

The theoretical possibilities are for an unchanged offer of repo funds at a fixed interest rate of three percent, for a fixed repo at a higher rate, for a variable rate repo where banks bid at different rate for funds or for a combination.
A variable rate repo would signal that the central bank was freeing up the rate to rise in line with a tigher money market.

Yet two weeks of frantic market speculation and scrutiny of snippets of statements from central bank council members has led to the conclusion that, for now, the central bank will do absolutely nothing that could give its policy new direction.
Indeed the overwhelming unanimity on this view appears in itself the main risk to the forecast, given that the Bundesbank always prefers to act when market expectations are low.

Analysts argue that the danger of any tightening move are just too high. A disturbance of equilibrium could even turn the currency markets back around, triggering a mark sell-off. And any move at all risks irritating Germany's European neighbours.
"The Bundesbank will not switch to an interest rate tender from a fixed rate tender this week as such a shift would hold more risks than opportunities," Bank Julius Baer said.
Hypo Research agreed, "We are assuming that there is no immediate pressure for the Bundesbank to act and that it will therefore stick with an unchanged policy."

The dollar, which hit a high above 1.89 marks last week after surging steadily from 1.54 at the start of the year, has now settled back to around 1.8850 marks, helped lower by the market taking a more critical view of sterling.

If no action is taken this week, the immediate focus will switch to August 21, when the central bank council resumes its regular meetings. A sudden policy change at next week's repo is seen very much as an outside chance.
Any delay in the decision strengthens the central bank's hand, giving it more scope to make a larger and more soundly justified upward move which will be hard for markets to ignore.

But August 21 is also by no means a certain date for a move, analysts said, with many predicting a policy change at some point over the next month or two but anticipating no real urgency for the central bank to act.

"The five-year period of falling German interest rates is nearly over. The Bundesbank likely will switch to a variable rate repurchase agreement in the next month or two and allow a gradual rise in the call rate for the first time since 1992," economists at Salomon Brothers said.
